evidence.claim: The Coastal Byway follows NH 1A and 1B between Portsmouth and Seabrook, overlooking sandy beaches, rocky Gulf of Maine shores and the Hampton Seabrook Marsh.
evidence.quote: The New Hampshire Coastal Byway follows NH Routes 1A & 1B 22 miles from Seabrook to Portsmouth . The Byway connects ten units of the State Park system as well as numerous local and private parks and recreational attractions. Historic structures along the route trace the history not only of the region but the country as a whole. The Byway overlooks the sandy beaches and rocky shores of the Gulf of Maine and the ecologically rich Hampton Seabrook Marsh.

evidence.quote: A new route to the island was created in 1821 when three bridges (now two bridges and a causeway) connected Frame Point in Portsmouth with the northwestern corner of Great Island.

evidence.quote: Previously, a bridge on the southwestern point had been the only way to reach New Castle without a boat.

evidence.claim: Travel south from Portsmouth on 1B across the causeway to New Castle, passing Fort Constitution and Fort Stark.
evidence.quote: Take Rt. 1B, which begins in Portsmouth's historic district, over the causeway to New Castle . This narrow route winds around the island, past the grand Wentworth-by-the-Sea and two early military fortifications, Fort Stark and Fort Constitution

evidence.claim: Join 1A for Odiorne Point, then follow the shore through Rye and North Hampton to Hampton Beach.
evidence.quote: When Rt. 1B connects with Rt. 1A, turn south through Rye and North Hampton to Hampton ; along the way you'll find Odiorne Point State Park and a series of State Parks with oceanfront beaches.

evidence.claim: Beyond the beach, Hampton Bridge carries the road across the harbor inlet to Seabrook.
evidence.quote: The Hampton Bridge carries Route 1A south across the Hampton Harbor inlet into Seabrook.

evidence.claim: The shore changes between sandy beaches and rock, with the Hampton Seabrook Marsh beside the byway.
evidence.quote: The Byway overlooks the sandy beaches and rocky shores of the Gulf of Maine and the ecologically rich Hampton Seabrook Marsh.

evidence.claim: The fort raided in December 1774 was called Fort William and Mary.
evidence.quote: Fort William and Mary was a colonial-era British fortress on the island of New Castle

evidence.claim: On December 14, John Langdon led Portsmouth-area Patriots against its six-man caretaker detachment and seized the gunpowder supply.
evidence.quote: On December 14, 1774, local Patriots from the Portsmouth area, led by local political leader and rebel activist John Langdon, stormed the post (overcoming a six-man caretaker detachment) and seized the garrison's gunpowder supply

evidence.claim: Rebels led by John Sullivan returned the next day for cannon, ammunition and supplies.
evidence.quote: On the following day, rebels led by colonial military officer John Sullivan again raided the fort, this time seizing with greater effort numerous heavy cannon, ammunition and supplies.

evidence.claim: The name Fort Constitution followed rebuilding completed in 1808.
evidence.quote: Work was completed in 1808 and the defense renamed "Fort Constitution".

evidence.claim: Workers doubled the height of the brick walls and added brick buildings inside, changing the colonial fort before its service in the War of 1812.
evidence.quote: Brick masonry walls were doubled in height, and new brick buildings were added inside.

evidence.claim: before its service in the War of 1812
evidence.quote: it was renamed Fort Constitution and served in the War of 1812.

evidence.claim: The site also holds Portsmouth Harbor Light, completed in 1878, continuing a lighthouse presence that began here in 1771.
evidence.quote: The fort has been home to a lighthouse since 1771.  The current installation, the Portsmouth Harbor Light, was completed in 1878.

evidence.claim: Fort Constitution was temporarily closed as of 2025.
evidence.quote: As of 2025 the park is temporarily closed.

evidence.claim: Circular concrete gun platforms remain at Odiorne Point, part of the former Fort Dearborn.
evidence.quote: The first battery at Fort Dearborn was called Battery Dearborn, and consisted of four 155 mm towed guns on "Panama mounts", which were circular concrete platforms. The platforms remain today.

evidence.claim: In 1942, the United States government condemned and bought private oceanfront property here to build coastal defenses.
evidence.quote: In 1942, during World War II, the site was condemned and purchased by the United States government for the construction of Fort Dearborn

evidence.claim: The guns themselves were scrapped in 1948, leaving the concrete structures as evidence of the military use of this shore.
evidence.quote: In 1948 Fort Dearborn was deactivated and all guns were scrapped.

evidence.claim: When the land passed to New Hampshire in 1961, former owners were not offered the chance to buy it back.
evidence.quote: In 1961 the site was ceded to the state of New Hampshire; the previous owners were not given the opportunity to re-purchase the land.

evidence.claim: The transfer required public recreation, and the park opened in July 1972.

evidence.claim: Hampton Beach occupies a barrier spit, with Hampton Harbor’s estuary separating most of the resort village from the mainland.
evidence.quote: Most of the resort village lies on a barrier spit separated from the mainland by a large estuary system known as Hampton Harbor.

evidence.claim: Ocean Boulevard runs along the beach beside the boardwalk.

evidence.claim: In the southern resort area, traffic divides between northbound Ocean Boulevard and southbound Ashworth Avenue, linked by cross streets lettered A through M.
evidence.quote: NH 1A splits into two one-way streets: the southbound Ashworth Avenue, and the northbound Ocean Boulevard. Cross streets through this area run from A Street in the north to M Street in the south.

evidence.claim: The village district was established in 1907 to bring electric power and water to the summer community.
evidence.quote: The Hampton Beach Village District was established on June 26, 1907, to provide electric power and water to the summer tourist community.

evidence.claim: North of the 101 and 1A junction, development thins into salt marsh, small businesses and bungalows.
evidence.quote: North of the junction of 101 and 1A, the area is much less developed, dominated mostly by a large salt marsh conservation area, with small businesses and bungalows along Ocean Boulevard (NH 1A).

evidence.claim: At the spit’s southern end, most of the land is state park, with little development.
evidence.quote: The southern end of the spit is mostly state park, with little to no buildings or development.

flags: Visit NH gives both 18.5 and 22 miles for the byway; catalog maps 26.5 miles. Distance omitted. The separate Colonial New Hampshire Seacoast Ride is 40 miles and extends inland; only its overlapping 1A/1B description is used.

No designation date or campaign history is cached. Official tourism pages identify the regional scenic byway; the history paragraph instead follows documented bridge connections without dating the entire corridor from those projects.

Fort Constitution source contradicts itself: lead says open, later section says temporarily closed as of 2025. Dated closure retained in practical; 2026 access unresolved without a saved manager update. Checked date records offline review. Do not advertise a walk inside.

Moments follow the main strip north-to-south: New Castle, Odiorne Point in Rye, Hampton Beach. Seabrook Beach’s separate 1.11-mile strip value is inconsistent with that sequence; geographic endpoint supported by cache.

All current landmark moments kept with exact titles, at and motifs where supplied. Current factual claims have cache support. The stone-throwing tavern account and Casino summer acts were omitted for focus, not because unsupported.
Fort Constitution rebuilding in 1808 distinguished from the colonial fort raided in 1774. Hampton Bridge’s 1901 wooden crossing distinguished from the 1949 replacement.
